meaning: A way libraries sort books by subject using numbers. Books on the same topic sit together on the shelf.
clues: It is a plan libraries use to decide where each book sits on the shelf.
It splits all subjects into ten big groups, numbered 000 to 900.
A library pioneer first published it in 1876.
Books about science sit in the 500s, and books about history sit in the 900s.
It has three words and eighteen letters, and the first word starts with D.
assumes: Library of Congress Classification call numbers start with a letter
A Cutter number only orders books within one subject
A card catalog lists books but does not set the shelf order

decoys.meaning: Another way libraries order books. It uses letters and numbers, so a book on education starts with L.
Drawers of small cards that described a library's books. People searched them to see what a library owned.
A short number added to a book's label. It puts books on the same subject in order, usually by the author's name.

exchange.speaker: floyd
exchange.text: Same subject, same shelf. You could wander along it and find neighbors you didn't know to ask for. Browsing still works.

exchange.speaker: bud
exchange.text: Today's version: the same system. Libraries around the world still use it to put books on the shelf.

exchange.speaker: floyd
exchange.text: Still, walk the shelves when you can. And a librarian will help you find your way.
